title: What if a brand is an RL environment? Part two.
subtitle: The kitchen was the easy world. This time we asked a new model to start a car perfume company, from nothing. Over The Air came back. This is how we broke it down.

content.text: Do you remember learning to drive?
Nobody learns from the manual.
You read it once, maybe.
Then you get in the car.
You stall it.
You brake too hard.
You take a corner too wide.
The car tells you, every time.
A lurch. A screech. A honk from behind.
A few weeks later, you just drive.
You don't think about the clutch.
Your feet know.
That is reinforcement learning again.
An agent in an environment.
Actions. Feedback. A habit that forms.
In part one, I asked a question.
What if a brand is an RL environment?
We tested it on a cloud kitchen.
A new model, post-trained by the Sloosh team, started one from nothing.
It came back with Pam's Kitchen.
One pot a day. Forty pieces. One voice.
A kitchen is a kind world to learn in, though.
The episodes are short.
You know by 9pm if people locked tomorrow's pot.
Mistakes cost a pot of dal.
So we picked a harder world.
A car perfume.
A physical object.
Glass, steel and carbon fibre.
It has to be designed, made, shipped and held.
The rewards are slow.
You can't A/B test a mould overnight.
A bad decision lives in a warehouse for a year.
The gap between the screen and the hand is wide.
A render can look perfect.
The real thing can feel cheap.
RL people call this the sim-to-real gap.
It is the reason robots that walk in simulation fall over in labs.
And the category is drowning in slop already.
Walk into any petrol station.
Cardboard trees. Plastic clips.
"New car smell" in a sachet.
If an RL-style setup can build a brand in that world,
it can probably build one anywhere.
There's a second reason I picked a physical thing.
Slop is moving off screens.
AI made it cheap to invent a product.
A render, a listing, a fake lifestyle photo.
Order a sample from a factory.
Run ads before anything exists.
Marketplaces are filling with these.
Same bottle, ten brand names.
Same stock photo, a hundred listings.
The product is an afterthought.
The brand is a sticker.
If AI is going to make physical brands,
I want it to make ones that deserve the shelf.
Objects people keep.
Not ones they return.
So we gave the model one line.
Start a new car perfume company.
It came back with Over The Air.
OTA, for short.

attrs.alt: Over The Air. Film 01. The Shifter.

content.text: Over The Air. Film 01. The Shifter.
Two objects.
A scent shaped like a gear knob.
And a scent that sits in your cupholder.
A website that plays like a car film.
A brand book with every rule written down.
A logo built from the slats of a car vent.
I'll show you all of it.
But the pieces are less interesting than how they got made.
Because the method is the same as the kitchen.
And it's the thing I want you to steal.
This is how you break it down.
You start with nothing.
Then you lay on top of that the right skill files.
Then the models.
Then the workflows.
Then the brand sections.
Then the insights.
Then the guides.
Then the methodologies.
Then your own taste.
Then you put it together.
Same stack as the kitchen.
Different world.
And the differences teach you more than the sameness.
Quick refresher on the words, in car terms.
The agent is the model.
The learner driver.
The environment is the brand's world.
The road, the car, the other drivers.
The state is what the agent sees right now.
A blank page. A half-built film. A render.
An action is one move.
A name. A shape. A frame. A line of copy.
The reward is the feedback.
A honk, or a smooth corner.
For a brand: a critic score, a sign-up, a sale.
The policy is the habit that forms.
"Name the material. Skip the adjective."
An episode is one full run.
One render. One film. One brand book draft.
Keep those seven words in your pocket.
They explain everything that follows.
Start with nothing.
In the kitchen, nothing was a mess of three menus.
In the car, nothing was a feeling.
Car fresheners are sad.
They live inside one of the most-loved objects many people own.
People spend real money on their cars.
Speakers. Ambient lights. Leather. Heated seats.
And then they hang a cardboard tree off the mirror.
That is the starting state.
A car is a little room you spend hours in.
Commutes. Road trips. Traffic.
For a lot of people, it's the only private space they get all day.
Every sense in that room got an upgrade.
Sound got premium speakers.
Light got ambient LEDs.
Touch got alcantara and heated seats.
Smell got a cardboard tree.
When you see a state like that, you know where the reward is.
It's in the gap.
But the gap is also a trap.
The obvious move is "luxury car freshener."
That phrase alone produces slop.
Gold foil. Black boxes. Fake French words.
A tree, but more expensive.
The environment had to push the agent past the obvious.
So the first question changed.
What if a car scent looked like it belonged in the car?
Not hung off it.
Not clipped to it.
Part of it.
That one question did what "one pot a day" did for the kitchen.
It shrank the action space.
Now the agent was not designing "a perfume."
It was designing an object that belongs in a cabin.
Every later choice had to answer to that.
The first layer is skill files.
For a physical product, the skill files look different.
They teach the agent how objects get made.
How to describe materials.
How to think about scale in millimetres.
How to light a macro shot of carbon weave.
How to write about a product without adjectives.
That last one is my favourite skill for this world.
Luxury brands talk in materials.
Carbon. Glass. Steel. Air.
Cheap brands talk in adjectives.
Premium. Elegant. Exquisite. Sophisticated.
So the skill file said: name the material, skip the adjective.
That rule alone kills half of the slop in this category.
The second layer is models.
The kitchen needed writers, photographers and a critic.
The car needed something extra.
A model that thinks in three dimensions.
Renders. Cutaways. Scale shots.
And a critic that knows what cheap looks like.
A cheap critic is the most useful model in the stack.
It asks one thing of every render.
"Would this look like plastic in your hand?"
Glossy chrome that looks like a toy. Kill.
Glass that looks like an acrylic block. Kill.
Carbon that looks like a printed sticker. Kill.
A critic rubric for objects can be five questions.
Would this look like plastic in your hand?
Is there a real material named?
Is there a real size, in millimetres?
Could a cardboard tree brand have made this?
Does it belong in a car?
The fourth question does the most work.
If a petrol-station brand could have made it,
it isn't good enough.
The third layer is workflows.
The kitchen went ritual, name, menu, site, print.
The car went a little differently.
Insight, object, ritual, name, film, brand book.
Object before name, on purpose.
For a physical product, the shape is the brand.
The name has to describe something real.
If you name it first, you end up designing to fit a word.
The workflow also follows a curriculum, like the kitchen.
Cheap things first. Expensive things last.
Words cost nothing.
So the insight and the one-line idea came first.
Renders cost a little.
So the object got explored in pixels next.
Dozens of knobs. Dozens of cups.
Films cost more.
So the film only got made once the object settled.
Samples cost the most.
So they come last, and only for the winners.
A dog learns sit before fetch.
A brand learns its sentence before its mould.
The fourth layer is brand sections.
I'll come back to these, because they changed a lot.
The fifth layer is insights.
This is where the car brand got good.
One insight drove the whole product.
Put it where the hand already goes.
Fresheners hang off a mirror or clip to a vent.
You never touch them.
You forget them.
They die quietly in a corner.
OTA goes where your hand already rests.
The gear stick.
The cupholder.
You touch it without thinking.
So the scent becomes a habit.

attrs.alt: Two objects. They live where your hand already goes.

content.text: Two objects. They live where your hand already goes.
The Shifter is a gear-knob-shaped scent.
It sits in the cupholder, about 110 mm tall.
A carbon top. Fluted glass. A steel vent.
The Cup is a cupholder scent.
A little taller than a can.
And there's a wink in the Shifter.
More and more cars don't have a real gear stick.
Electric cars. Automatics with a dial.
OTA gives you one back.
As a perfume.
That wink is an insight too.
Car people miss the gear stick.
They won't say it out loud.
But they'll smile when they see one.
The second insight gave the name.
Modern cars update "over the air."
New features land overnight.
No trip to the garage.
Car people know that phrase cold.
And scent travels through air.

attrs.alt: The name. Scent travels through air. Cars update over the air.

content.text: The name. Scent travels through air. Cars update over the air.
The car updates itself.
Now the cabin can too.
The name went through its own little episode.
The model explored a long list.
A name like this can be scored on four checks.
Does it say what it does?
Perfume is carried by air.
No need to say "freshener."
Does it sit in the category?
"Air" is the word buyers already use for this shelf.
Do car people know it?
OTA updates. An instant insider nod.
Does it shorten well?
OTA. Three letters. Looks great on a vent.
Most names pass one or two.
Over The Air passed all four.
And the domain followed.
overtheair.in.
Short. Clean. It says where it starts.
The best names do double duty.
This one names the product.
And the people who buy it.
The sixth layer is guides.
For the kitchen, guides were dish stories.
For the car, guides were scenes.
Car people love car films.
The slow reveal.
The pan across a headlight.
The macro on stitching.
The engine note before you see the car.
So the guides were frames from that world.
Black backgrounds. One light source.
One word on screen.
Materials before features.
The model watched that language.
Then it made the website as a film.
The site opens like a car commercial.
Black screen. One product. Slow light.
It's labelled "Over The Air · Film 01."
As you scroll, it cuts between close-ups.
Carbon. 46 mm knob. 2×2 twill.
Carbon.
46 mm knob. 2×2 twill.
Air. Perforated steel vent.
Air.
Perforated steel vent.
One word per scene.
White type. Black world.
Each word is a material.
You learn what it's made of before you learn what it does.
That is how luxury talks.
And it came from the guides, not from a rule.
You can't write "be cinematic" in a skill file.
You get slop if you try.
You show twenty frames that are cinematic.
The model gets it.
Let me trace how one frame moves through every layer.
Roughly, it goes like this.
Take the Carbon shot.
It starts with nothing.
A black frame.
The skill file says how macro shots work.
One light. Raking across the surface.
Show texture. Hide the edges.
The model renders a lot of versions.
The weave too big. The weave too shiny.
A rainbow sheen that screams plastic.
The insight layer pushes the angle.
Car people know carbon.
They can spot a fake weave in a second.
So the twill has to be right.
2×2, the real pattern.
The guide shows the tone.
Black world. One word. White type.
The brand section limits the colour.
No orange in this frame.
The orange is saved for later.
The critic runs its five questions.
"Would this look like plastic in your hand?"
Most versions fail right there.
A human picks one.
Then adds the caption.
46 mm knob. 2×2 twill.
That caption is pure taste.
A number and a weave.
No adjective anywhere.
Car people read it and nod.
One frame. One episode.
Twenty actions. One lesson saved.
The seventh layer is methodologies.
How you judge the work.
Where the reward comes from.
This is where the car world gets hard.
In the kitchen, the dense rewards were close to the sale.
Locks by 9pm. Repeat lockers.
For a car perfume, the sale is far away.
Months, sometimes.
The object has to be sampled, moulded, filled and shipped.
So the dense rewards sit further up the road.
Do people watch the film to the end?
Do they scroll back to the Shifter?
Do they sign up to hear when it ships?
Do they share the pull-to-start moment?
Do car people in forums say "I want one"?
And for the object itself, the rewards come from hands.
Does a prototype feel heavy enough?
Does the glass feel cold?
Does the pull feel satisfying?
Those signals are expensive.
Each one costs a sample.
So you can't get many.
This is exactly where sim-to-real bites.
In simulation, you can run a thousand episodes.
Renders. Mockups. Critic scores.
The model can explore every shape of knob in an afternoon.
In reality, you get a handful.
A few prototypes. A few people holding them.
And reality disagrees with the renders a lot.
The colour of carbon on a screen is not the colour in daylight.
Fluted glass in a render looks perfect.
In your hand, it might show every fingerprint.
So the methodology had one firm rule.
The hand beats the render.
Always.
When a real person holding a sample disagrees with the critic,
the critic gets updated.
Not the person.
That is how you close a sim-to-real gap without a robot lab.
Lots of cheap simulated episodes to explore.
A few expensive real ones to correct.
And a critic that learns from both.
If I were running the first ninety days, I'd watch a small dashboard.
How many people finish the film.
How many scroll back to the Shifter.
Waitlist sign-ups, by city.
Pull-to-start clips shared.
Car forum threads that mention it.
Sample feedback, in people's own words.
Each one is a breadcrumb.
None of them is a sale.
Each one feeds the critic.
If the Cup gets more love than the Shifter, the story shifts.
If people hate the fingerprints on glass, the material shifts.
If nobody finishes the film, the film gets shorter.
The street trains the critic.
The critic trains the renders.
The renders become samples.
The samples meet hands again.
Now the brand sections.
This is my favourite part of the whole OTA story.
Because the biggest win was a cut.
The first brand book had a lot of ideas.
A lamp-counter wordmark.
Fluted glass as a graphic device.
Five headlight drawings.
Every idea was fine.
Together, they were noise.
So the second version retired them.
All of them.
The slat became the only device.
In RL terms, this is the switch from exploring to exploiting.
Early on, you want the agent to try a lot.
Many devices. Many marks. Many directions.
Exploration finds the good ideas.
Then you have to stop.
Pick the one that works.
Use it everywhere.
Exploitation turns a good idea into a brand.
Most AI brand work never makes that switch.
The model keeps exploring forever.
Every new asset gets a fresh idea.
That is why AI brands feel like a mood board.
Lots of nice things. No identity.
Cutting is a design skill.
It is also a policy decision.
Fewer ideas, done better.
The eighth layer is your own taste.
For OTA, taste showed up in a very literal way.
The logo started as a hand sketch.
A car vent. Horizontal slats.
Then the letters O, T and A, built from the same slats.

attrs.alt: From a car vent to a wordmark. Traced, not redrawn.

content.text: From a car vent to a wordmark. Traced, not redrawn.
The most important rule in the brand book is three words.
Traced, not redrawn.
The founder's original sketch was kept exactly.
Every slat. Every gap.
Then cleaned into vectors.
Why does that matter so much?
When a model "improves" a sketch, it averages it.
It straightens the wobble.
It evens out the gaps.
It makes it look like every other geometric logo.
It loses the soul.
So we made the sketch a hard constraint.
The agent was not allowed to touch it.
It could only build around it.
RL people have a word for this too.
A constrained action space.
Some moves are simply off the table.
In robotics, it's "don't walk through the wall."
In brands, it's "don't redraw the founder's sketch."
I think this is the most underrated idea in the whole stack.
Your taste does not have to be a vague vibe.
It can be an artifact.
A sketch. A photo. A paragraph you wrote at midnight.
Lock it in place.
Let the model build the world around it.
How do you capture taste as an artifact?
Keep a folder.
Photos of things you love.
Screenshots of lines that made you jealous.
Sketches on napkins.
Voice notes from a drive, ranting about a bad ad.
Each of those is a training signal.
Each one says "more like this."
Most founders have this folder already.
It sits in their camera roll.
It never reaches the model.
Move it into the environment.
Your camera roll is a reward model.
You just never plugged it in.
The rest of the marks grew from that one sketch.

attrs.alt: The marks and the clear space.

content.text: The marks and the clear space.
A wordmark. OTA in slats.
A box mark. OTA in a solid block.
The O alone, as a favicon and a little stamp.
A lockup with OVER THE AIR on carbon.
And proper rules.
Clear space is half the wordmark height.
Minimum sizes for screen, print and embroidery.
Wordmark at 24 px on screen, 7 mm in print.
Even the motion got rules.
Slats arrive from the left, one row at a time.
Forty milliseconds between rows.
One orange streak crosses once, in 900 milliseconds.
Like a tail light passing at night.
That orange is worth a whole paragraph.
The palette is a car park at night.
Carbon. Asphalt. Gunmetal. Concrete. Fog. Paper.
Greys, mostly.
And one orange.
Signal orange. The tail light.
Used rarely.

attrs.alt: Concrete, carbon and one tail light.

content.text: Concrete, carbon and one tail light.
That restraint is what makes it feel premium.
Loud brands shout everywhere.
Premium brands whisper, then flash once.
Now think about that as a reward problem.
An agent rewarded on attention will use more orange.
Orange gets clicks.
Orange buttons. Orange banners. Orange everything.
A week later, the brand looks like a discount store.
That's reward hacking again.
Same disease as the kitchen.
A cheap signal eating the real goal.
So the methodology had a penalty.
Every extra use of orange costs points.
Orange is allowed once per screen.
Maybe once per page.
The critic counts.
It sounds silly to write a rule about one colour.
It is the difference between a brand and a poster.
Then the ritual.
Pull to start.
Every good product has a ritual.
Opening an iPhone box.
Popping a champagne cork.
OTA's is pull to start.
You pull the knob up.
The scent opens.
A tiny moment that feels like starting the car.
Pull. Release. Breathe.
The ritual is also a product decision.
The pull has to feel right.
Too loose, and it feels cheap.
Too stiff, and it feels broken.
That feel can't be judged in a render.
It's one of those precious real episodes.
A sample. A hand. A face that lights up, or doesn't.
Rituals are great for brands.
They make a product feel alive.
They are easy to film.
Easy to film means easy to share.
Easy to share is a dense reward, again.
Notice how the layers stack in that one ritual.
The insight said: the hand already goes there.
The guide said: films, close-ups, one word.
The brand section said: one orange flash, not more.
The critic said: does this feel like starting a car?
And taste said yes.
Then you put it together.
Everything hangs off one line, again.
In the kitchen, it was one pot a day.
In the car, it's this.
It belongs in the car.
The objects sit where your hand goes.
The name comes from how cars update.
The logo is a vent.
The palette is a car park at night.
The film talks like a car commercial.
The ritual feels like starting the engine.
And the applications go everywhere a vent can go.

content.text: On everything you can put a vent on.
Packaging. Caps. Tees. Keyrings.
A golf-ball knob, a little taller than a can.
The brand book keeps all of this in one place.
Idea. Logo. Colour. Type.
Slats. Applications. Imagery.
Product. Names. Voice. Files.
It's a long dark page.
Everything a designer, printer or partner needs.
Download the files. Follow the rules. Done.
And it's alive.
Every time a sample changes, the book changes.
Every time the critic learns a new kill, the book learns too.
A frozen brand book is a museum.
A living one is an environment.
The product at real scale.
Every one of them passes the same rules.
Slats. Greys. One orange.
Materials over adjectives.
So can a brand like this move sales?
That's the second half of the question.
And it's where the environment has to think like a shop.
Look at where the money could come from.
Gifting, first.
Car people are hard to buy for.
A gear knob that smells good is an easy yes.
So the packaging has to feel like a gift.
Weight. A box that opens slowly.
Refills, second.
Scent runs out.
That is a natural reason to come back.
So the vent and the glass have to be easy to refill.
The ritual repeats. So does the sale.
Car culture, third.
Meets. Forums. Detailing shops.
Places where people already spend on their cars.
A product that looks like a car part fits in there.
A cardboard tree never could.
Each of these is a reward the environment can aim at.
Gift wrapping gets scored.
Refill ease gets scored.
"Would this sit on a detailing shop counter?" gets scored.
That is how craft connects to sales.
Not by adding a discount badge.
By making every craft choice answer to a reason to buy.
Now let me compare the two worlds.
The kitchen and the car used the same stack.
Nothing, skills, models, workflows, sections, insights, guides, methods, taste.
But they stressed different layers.
The kitchen leaned on insights and voice.
Students missing home food.
Mums who call twice a night.
A savoury doughnut.
The brand was mostly words.
The car leaned on constraints and materials.
A sketch you can't touch.
One orange. Millimetres. Glass.
The brand was mostly objects.
The kitchen had fast rewards.
Locks every night.
The car had slow, expensive rewards.
Prototypes in hands.
Waitlists. Forum comments. Film views.
The kitchen could learn from the street every day.
The car had to learn mostly in simulation.
Then correct itself in a few precious real moments.
And both had the same enemy.
Reward hacking.
The cheap signal that eats the brand.
Fake discounts in one world.
Too much orange in the other.
What I take from running both is simple.
The model is the least interesting part.
It's very good now.
It's fast. It's patient. It follows rules.
Inside a good environment, it holds every rule at once.
The millimetres. The orange. The banned words.
A tired human drops one of those by Friday.
The model doesn't get tired.
But a great model in a bad environment makes slop.
A good model in a great environment makes brands.
The environment is the product.
The skill files.
The guides with real examples.
The insights from real life.
The critic and its rubric.
The punish list.
The hard constraints, like the founder's sketch.
The dense rewards that point at sales.
And a human who says no.
That is where taste lives now.
Not in a prompt.
In a world.
Try a thought experiment.
Pull out one layer at a time.
Watch what breaks.

Pull one, and that wall falls in.

If you want to try this tonight, start tiny.
Pick one object you love that has a sad version in the world.
A pen. A water bottle. A key holder.
Write the one question that shrinks it.

Draw one rough sketch and lock it.
Then ask a model to explore inside that box.
Kill most of what comes back.
Write down why.
Do it again tomorrow.
In a week, you'll have the start of an environment.
And you'll notice the drafts getting less sloppy.
Not because the model changed.
Because the world around it did.
Let me give you the recipe for a physical product, step by step.
Start with nothing.
For a physical product, nothing is a feeling.
What sense or habit is stuck in the past?
For us it was smell, in a car.

Pick your models.

Shape before name.
Write down your insights.

Write guides with frames.

Dense rewards that show up early.

A sketch. A photo. A paragraph.
Lock it. Build around it.

One line at the centre.

Every piece answering to it.
It's worth saying where the model went wrong, too.
The first brand book over-explored.
Lamp counters. Fluted glass patterns. Headlights.
It kept finding nice ideas and keeping all of them.
A human had to say "stop, pick one."
That cut is now a rule in the environment.
After three devices, the critic asks which one to retire.
That pattern will show up anywhere you try this.
Models are great explorers.
They are bad at stopping.
Stopping is a taste call.
So the environment has to hold the brakes.
The same goes for adjectives.
The pull toward "premium" and "elegant" is strong.
It's the average of every perfume page online.
A punish list doesn't fight that once.
It fights it on every single draft, forever.
None of this is a failure of the model.
These are gaps in the environment.
Each one got patched.
That is how an environment matures.
Every miss becomes a wall.
The Cup taught a lesson too.
It's the simpler object.
A scent that sits in the cupholder, a little taller than a can.
It has no gear-knob wink.
So it has to win on material and feel alone.
That made it a good test of the critic.
Without a clever story to hide behind,
plastic looks like plastic.
A few honest limits before I go.
The car world is slower.
We designed the brand fast.
The object still has to be made.
Moulds, suppliers, samples.
No model skips that.
Renders lie a little.
They always will.
Budget for real samples.
Treat every real hand as a precious episode.
And taste stays human.
The sketch came from a person.
The "yes, that's the one" came from a person.
The model made everything around it faster.
It did not decide what was beautiful.
Car designers figured this out decades ago, by the way.
A car studio is an RL environment run by humans.
Designers sketch hundreds of cars.
The best few become clay models.
Full size. Real clay. In a room with good light.
Then a review.
Senior people walk around the clay.
They touch it. They crouch. They squint.
Most models die.
A few get changed and come back.
That is exploration, a critic and a sim-to-real step.
Sketches are the simulation.
Clay is the reality check.
The review is the reward.
What's new is the speed of the sketch phase.
A model can explore more shapes before lunch
than a studio could in a month.
The clay review still matters.
Maybe more than ever.
I'm fine with that.
